title.en: Who gives you milk, makes your shoes and teaches you?

text.en: A dairy farmer, a shoemaker and a teacher each work in a different sector of the economy. Today we classify economic work and see why jobs matter.

The primary sector uses natural resources, as in agriculture and dairy. The secondary sector turns raw material into goods, and the tertiary sector provides services such as transport, banking and teaching.
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year. Only final goods are counted to avoid double counting.
Over time the tertiary sector has become the largest in GDP, but most workers are still employed in agriculture.
Underemployment or disguised unemployment occurs when more people work than are needed, as when five family members work on land that needs two.
In the organised sector, jobs are regular and protected by laws. In the unorganised sector, jobs are irregular, wages are low and there is little protection.
The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005 guarantees 100 days of employment in a year in rural areas.
The public sector is owned and run by the government, while the private sector is owned by individuals or companies.
The government supports sectors through irrigation, procurement and employment schemes so that the poor are protected.

problem.en: A village produces 400 kg wheat and 100 kg flour from it. Why count only the flour in GDP if both are final?

text.en: Wheat used to make flour is an intermediate good.

why.en: It is used in producing flour.

text.en: Counting both would double count the wheat value.

prompt.en: Explain the difference between organised and unorganised sectors.

requiredIdeas.en: Organised jobs are regular and protected
Unorganised jobs are irregular and unprotected

points.en: There are three sectors: primary, secondary, tertiary.
GDP counts final goods and services.
